title: 1:1 Meeting Notes
description: Managers: recurring one-to-ones with mood, agenda and action items per person.

spec.useCase: Ruth Abernathy manages three engineers and uses this to keep a steady one to one rhythm and not lose any promise she made.

text.text: A steady rhythm of one to ones beats occasional big talks. Add a meeting after each conversation, write down actions, and check the open list before the next one.

Pick one or two questions per conversation. The best question is often the plainest, and silence after it is part of the method.
Pick one or two. The best question is often the plainest.
Check-in
What is on your mind this week?
What was the best part of your week?
What is draining your energy?
Work
What would you do differently on the current project?
What is blocking you that I could remove?
Growth
What do you want to learn in the next three months?
What kind of work do you want more of?
Feedback
What could I do to be a better manager for you?
What feedback have you been holding back?
When something is wrong
What is one thing that would make your week easier?
Is there anything you expected to hear from me that you have not?
What did you decide not to tell me last time?
When things are going well
What are you most proud of since we last spoke?
What would you like to do more of?
How to run the conversation
Let them go first and take notes; do not rush to fix.
Say back what you heard before you respond.
End by agreeing two actions, one each.
Mood is each person's own 1 to 5 rating at the end of the meeting. The trend matters more than any single number.
A run of low moods is a reason to meet sooner, not later.
How to read the trends
A mood of 2 or below twice in a row: talk about workload before anything else.
Many open actions on your side: you are the bottleneck; clear them first.
Moods rising after a project change: write down what changed.
